source.title: LoRA's Second Descent Extends Beyond Parameter Parity

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent corruption or truncation.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how training fit and test risk change under label noise in LoRA rank sweeps, using a different model setup from the original random-label experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper studies partial label corruption and adapter-rank sweeps. It does not report a completely random labeling of the full training set, shuffled or Gaussian-noise inputs, or training-time comparisons for fitting random versus true labels. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study measures fitting of partially randomized labels and generalization as corruption increases in pretrained networks with LoRA adapters. These results bear on V4 in a new training setting. It does not test fully random labels or the regularization claims in V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find a second descent along LoRA rank, but no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters matches module-matched dense risk. The first equivalence result requires four times dense projection weights under a shared learning rate; rank-one adaptation offers the strongest parameter advantage.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LoRA fine-tuning of pretrained vision and language models under partial label noise, with rank sweeps and module-matched dense comparisons; it does not reproduce full random-label training of standard networks.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise rate changes cliff amplitude; augmentation reduces it; training budget moves the peak; model, backbone, rank grid, learning rate, weight decay, scaling, and adapter placement affect reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA interpolates CIFAR-100N human annotations at sufficiently large ranks while test NLL worsens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretrained networks with sufficiently expressive adapters can memorize human annotation errors.

fits_no_version.finding: Augmentation reduces the NLL cliff, while changing weight decay preserves its valley and peak locations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The rank-dependent generalization cliff under partial label noise persists across these augmentation and weight-decay settings.

record.problems: The noise-rate sweep ends at 60%, not complete random labeling. Some robustness outcomes are reported only as plotted curves. The Qwen2.5-7B comparisons share three seeds, described by the authors as descriptive. The weight-decay comparison uses different effective regularizers for dense and LoRA arms.
record.rows_left_out: Selected results directly relevant to V4 and V5 are included. Other rank-by-rank values and experiments on dense axes, frozen factors, optimizer coordinates, calibration, and model selection were left out because they do not directly measure the stated versions' outcomes.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, chance test performance, and fitting without changing architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training-time ratios for true versus random labels and convergence slowing with increasing corruption.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
The full none-to-all corruption trajectory, perfect training fit at every corruption rate, and classification error steadily approaching chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent fitting completely random labels; whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Within-training ordering of learning real patterns and memorizing corrupted labels.

missing.what: Matched clean-versus-20%-corrupted training and test accuracy. At r=64 both conditions reach 100% training accuracy, while test accuracy falls from 65.0% clean to 53.9% noisy; at r=192 it falls from 65.7% to 55.4%. These directly establish degradation under corruption more clearly than NLL alone.
Qwen2.5-7B fits 20%-corrupted AG News labels to 100% training accuracy at r≥64, versus 80.7% at r=1. This extends the partial-noise interpolation result to language-model fine-tuning.

record.verdict_notes: Incomplete experimental coverage does not itself warrant limits_scope. The original V5 verdict should be removed because persistence of a generalization curve does not measure the random-label fitting behavior V5 names.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling of the training set is tested.
No training-time comparison between fitting random and true labels is reported.
No shuffled-pixel or Gaussian-noise input experiment is reported.
The noise-rate sweep reaches 60%, not 100%; no result establishes behavior across the full none-to-all range.

Dropout and the claimed effect of removing regularization on generalization with true labels are not tested. Random-label fitting is not tested; augmentation and weight decay are studied under partial label noise.
The paper does not measure whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: ImageNet-1k-pretrained DeiT-Tiny
rows.operation_detail: LoRA rank sweep on the fused qkv projections of the last six blocks, with 20% symmetric label noise.
rows.measure: Train accuracy and test NLL across ranks; train accuracy reaches 99% between r=16 and r=24 while test NLL peaks at r=64.
rows.value: At r=64: test NLL 2.102±.020; train accuracy 100%. At r=192: test NLL 2.069±.023; train accuracy 100%.
rows.uncertainty: Mean±std over 5 seeds for the main sweep.
rows.note: Shows interpolation of a partially corrupted training set and increased test NLL; this is not a fully random labeling.
rows.check: The numbers are correct, but distinguish ranks: training accuracy is 74.6% at r=1 and 100% at r≥32. This measures interpolation at 20% corruption, not the complete noise-rate trajectory. Increasing rank is not increasing corruption.

rows.subject: ImageNet-1k-pretrained DeiT-Tiny
rows.operation_detail: LoRA rank sweep while varying the symmetric label-noise fraction.
rows.measure: Test NLL curve across rank; the valley stays at r=1 and cliff amplitude grows monotonically with noise rate.
rows.note: Text describes the trend, but values are shown only in the figure. The experiment stops at 60% corruption.
rows.check: The noise-rate trend bears on V4, but the reported curves measure test NLL, not classification error approaching chance. They do not establish perfect training fit at every noise rate. Table 2 reports 3–5 seeds for the noise-rate experiments.

source_check.correct: Table 2 reports 3–5 seeds for E20, the noise-rate sweep; the 20% main-sweep reference uses 5 seeds.
source_check.locator_found: Table 2, E20 and E1; Section 5.6; Appendix E.1; Figure 11(a).
source_check.problem: The seed count is reported, contrary to seeds=not stated.

rows.subject: DeiT-Tiny
rows.operation_detail: LoRA rank sweep on CIFAR-100N with human re-annotation labels.
rows.measure: Test NLL and train accuracy across rank; test NLL has a valley at r=1 and peak at r=64, while train accuracy reaches 100% at r=64 and above.
rows.baseline: r=1 valley: test NLL 1.743±.017; train accuracy 72.7%.
rows.value: r=64 peak: test NLL 2.408±.020; train accuracy 100%; r=384: test NLL 2.350±.027; train accuracy 100%.
rows.note: Human label noise is not fully random relabeling; the paper describes it as approximately 40%.
rows.check: The numerical extraction is correct, but human annotation errors are not randomly corrupted labels. A rank sweep at one human-noise level cannot establish V4's random-corruption trajectory.

rows.subject: ImageNet-1k-pretrained DeiT-Tiny
rows.operation_detail: Repeated noisy-label LoRA rank sweep with data augmentation.

conditions.value: random flip, pad-and-crop, and mixup α=0.2

rows.measure: Test NLL across rank; augmentation shrinks the curve's amplitude without changing its shape or adding a second descent.
rows.note: The paper reports the qualitative comparison in text and displays the curves in the figure.
rows.check: Persistence of a test-NLL cliff under augmentation does not establish that augmentation fails to prevent random-label fitting. No augmented training-fit result or fully random-label condition is reported. Table 2 specifies two seeds.

rows.subject: ImageNet-1k-pretrained DeiT-Tiny
rows.operation_detail: LoRA rank sweep at different weight-decay coefficients.
rows.measure: Test NLL and rank of valley and peak; at coefficients 0 and 10⁻¹ the valley remains r=1 and peak r=64. At r=d, LoRA finishes 0.08 nats above dense at each coefficient tested.
rows.baseline: Weight decay 10⁻²; comparison to coefficients 0 and 10⁻¹.
rows.value: At weight decay 0 and 10⁻¹, the sweep keeps its valley at r=1 and peak at r=64; at r=d LoRA is 0.08 nats above dense for coefficients 0, 10⁻² and 10⁻¹.
rows.uncertainty: Two seeds for the stated rank sweeps; three seeds for dense comparison.
rows.note: Equal coefficients define different regularizers for dense fine-tuning and ordinary LoRA, as the authors note.
rows.check: The weight-decay results concern test NLL and LoRA-versus-dense differences under 20% corruption. They do not report random-label fitting or generalization after removing regularization on true labels, so they cannot establish V5.

relationships.condition: DeiT-Tiny, CIFAR-100, 20% symmetric corruption, LoRA r≥32 at 40 epochs
relationships.reason: R1 reports 100% training accuracy despite corruption; Table 8 also shows worse test accuracy than clean-label training at matched ranks. This supports the interpolation and degradation components in this setting.
relationships.display_finding: Training accuracy reached 100%, while test accuracy was worse than clean-label training at matched ranks.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: DeiT-Tiny, CIFAR-100, 20% symmetric corruption, LoRA r≥32 at 40 epochs
source_check.reason: R1 and Table 8 show 100% training accuracy at the measured ranks and lower test accuracy than matched clean-label training; this supports the tested partial-noise setting.

relationships.condition: DeiT-Tiny with low-rank adapters at a fixed 40-epoch budget
relationships.reason: R1 shows training accuracy of only 74.6% at r=1 and 98.0% at r=16 under 20% corruption; perfect fitting depends on adapter capacity and budget.
relationships.display_finding: At 20% corruption, training accuracy reached 74.6% with rank 1 and 98.0% with rank 16.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: DeiT-Tiny with low-rank adapters at a fixed 40-epoch budget
source_check.reason: R1 shows incomplete fitting at r=1 and r=16, while higher ranks interpolate, establishing dependence on adapter capacity within the fixed budget.

relationships.condition: DeiT-Tiny synthetic corruption sweep from 10% to 60%
relationships.reason: R2 reports monotonically increasing test-NLL cliff amplitude with corruption, supporting noise-dependent degradation over the measured range.
relationships.display_finding: The amplitude of the cliff in test negative log-likelihood increased monotonically with label corruption.

relation.reason: The study measures noisy-label training accuracy and clean-test performance, providing direct component evidence on V4.

tranche.reason: Pretrained networks with LoRA adapters provide a new training setting with results on partial-noise fitting and generalization.

source_check.notes: The study does not establish perfect fitting throughout a 0–100% corruption sweep or classification error approaching chance. Appendix C.3 confirms the unextracted Qwen2.5-7B result; the authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate.

statements.correction: Table 8: 20% corruption, 40 epochs; training accuracy 74.6% at r=1, 98.0% at r=16, 99.9% at r=24, and 100% at measured r≥32. Verdict: limits_scope for low-rank adapters within this budget.
statements.problem: The DeiT-Tiny numbers are correct, but labeling these capacity-dependent incomplete fits as challenges overstates the result under the verdict rules.

reader_labels.reason: The reported experiments show training interpolation with rising test NLL under partial corruption, but do not establish the version's full none-to-all noise range or its claim across all corruption levels; see R1–R3.
